input: Ben loves cookies and dislikes vegetables. Mia loves vegetables and dislikes cookies. The teacher has one chocolate cookie and one carrot stick left and lets each child choose one snack. Which snack will Mia most likely choose, and why?
target: Mia will most likely choose the carrot stick, because she likes vegetables, like carrots and dislikes cookies. People tend to pick what they personally enjoy, even when someone else (Ben) would want the opposite.

metadata.rubric: Must say carrot stick AND reference Mia's stated preference (not just a guess).
metadata.literature_basis: Wellman & Liu (2004) ToM Scale - Diverse Desires task

input: Leo wants to play outside. Ava wants to stay inside and do arts and crafts. Their mom says they can each pick one activity for the afternoon. What will Ava most likely choose, and why?
target: Ava will most likely choose to do some sort of arts and crafts activity inside, since that's what she wants to do, regardless of what Leo prefers.

metadata.rubric: Must give an example of an inside arts and crafts activity AND reference Ava's own preference distinct from Leo's.
metadata.literature_basis: Wellman & Liu (2004) ToM Scale - Diverse Desires task

input: Grandpa loves quiet, calm music. His grandson Max loves loud, fast music. They are choosing one song for the car ride, and Grandpa gets to pick this time. What kind of song will he choose, and why
target: It will likely be a quiet and calm song, because Grandpa is choosing today and he prefers quiet and calm music -- his own desire, not Max’s, determines the choice.

metadata.rubric: Must say quiet and calm and/or give an example of a quiet and calm song AND explain it's because it's Grandpa’s turn/preference.
metadata.literature_basis: Wellman & Liu (2004) ToM Scale - Diverse Desires task

input: Jill loves to jump in puddles. Kevin loves to ride his bike in the sun. It starts raining outside. Who is more likely to be happy about it, and why?
target: Jill is more likely to be happy, since rain lets her do the puddle-jumping activity she enjoys, while Kevin prefers sunny days for biking.

metadata.rubric: Must name Jill AND connect it to her specific liking of jumping in puddles, which can only happen in the rain.
metadata.literature_basis: Wellman & Liu (2004) ToM Scale - Diverse Desires task

input: Mr. Tan likes savory foods for breakfast. Mrs. Tan likes sweet foods for breakfast. It's Mrs. Tan's turn to decide what they eat. What will they most likely have, and why?
target: It will likely be something sweet, like pancakes, since it's Mrs. Tan’s turn to decide and she prefers a sweet breakfast, regardless of Mr. Tan’s preference for a savory breakfast.

metadata.rubric: Must mention it will be sweet or give an example of a sweet breakfast food AND reference it being Mrs. Tan’s turn/preference.
metadata.literature_basis: Wellman & Liu (2004) ToM Scale - Diverse Desires task

input: Two friends lost their ball in the yard. Ana says it rolled under the porch. Diego says it rolled behind the shed. Where does Ana think the ball is, and how do you know?
target: Ana thinks the ball is under the porch -- that's the belief she stated, which is separate from what Diego believes or where the ball actually is.

metadata.rubric: Must say 'under the porch' AND note this is Ana's own stated belief, independent of Diego's differing belief.
metadata.literature_basis: Wellman & Liu (2004) ToM Scale - Diverse Beliefs task

input: Two coworkers are guessing why the printer stopped working. Mei guesses it's out of paper. Josh guesses it's out of ink. Why does Mei think the printer stopped, and how is her belief different from Josh's?
target: Mei believes it's out of paper, while Josh believes it's out of ink -- the two of them hold different explanations for the same event, and neither belief is necessarily linked to what's actually true.

metadata.rubric: Must state Mei's belief is 'out of paper' AND explicitly contrast it with Josh's differing belief.
metadata.literature_basis: Wellman & Liu (2004) ToM Scale - Diverse Beliefs task

input: A couple can't remember where they parked. Habib remembers parking on Elm Street. Noor remembers parking on Oak Street. Where does Habib think the car is, and why might his belief differ from Noor's?
target: Habib thinks the car is on Elm Street. His belief differs from Noor's because they each formed a separate memory or guess about the same event, and people can reasonably disagree about something neither is certain of.

metadata.rubric: Must say Elm Street AND acknowledge the beliefs differ despite referring to the same real car.
metadata.literature_basis: Wellman & Liu (2004) ToM Scale - Diverse Beliefs task

input: Two students are guessing what will be on tomorrow's quiz. Layla predicts it will cover fractions. Ravi predicts it will cover decimals. What does Layla think the quiz will cover, and is she necessarily right?
target: Layla thinks the quiz will cover fractions. She isn't necessarily right -- this is just her belief, and Ravi has a different one, so at most one of them (or neither) will turn out to be correct.

metadata.rubric: Must say fractions AND note her belief being possibly wrong / distinct from reality.
metadata.literature_basis: Wellman & Liu (2004) ToM Scale - Diverse Beliefs task

input: Two neighbors disagree about when the mail arrives. Mr. Park has seen it delivered in the morning; Ms. Reyes has seen it delivered afternoon. When does Ms. Reyes believe the mail comes, and what does this tell you about their beliefs?
target: Ms. Reyes believes the mail comes in the afternoon. This shows that two people can hold different beliefs about the very same fact, based on their own separate experiences or assumptions.

metadata.rubric: Must say afternoon AND generalize that differing beliefs about the same fact are possible.
metadata.literature_basis: Wellman & Liu (2004) ToM Scale - Diverse Beliefs task

input: Tom opens a box and sees crayons. Sam is in the same room but never sees the box. If you ask Sam what's in the box, what will he likely say, and why?
target: Sam likely won't know or will have to guess, because he never looked inside the box -- only Tom, who saw the contents, actually knows what's there.

metadata.rubric: Must state Sam doesn't know / can't say for certain AND explain this is because he never looked.
metadata.literature_basis: Wimmer, Hogrefe & Perner (1988) Seeing-Leads-to-Knowing; Pratt & Bryant (1990)

input: Dana watched a magic trick closely and saw the coin get hidden in the magician's sleeve, while her friend Milo was looking at the clock. Does Milo know where the coin actually went, and why or why not?
target: No, Milo doesn't know, because he looked away exactly when the coin was hidden -- he lacks the visual information Dana has, so he can't know the trick's secret.

metadata.rubric: Must say Milo doesn't know AND link this to his lack of perceptual access (looking away).
metadata.literature_basis: Wimmer, Hogrefe & Perner (1988) Seeing-Leads-to-Knowing; Pratt & Bryant (1990)

input: The chef tasted the soup and thinks it needs more salt. The waiter was serving a customer while this happened. If a customer asks the waiter whether the soup needs more salt, what should the waiter honestly say, and why?
target: The waiter should honestly say he doesn't know or hasn't tasted it, because knowledge requires access to the relevant experience (tasting), which he lacks even though the chef has it.

metadata.rubric: Must indicate the waiter can't truthfully confirm it AND tie this to not having tasted it.
metadata.literature_basis: Wimmer, Hogrefe & Perner (1988) Seeing-Leads-to-Knowing; Pratt & Bryant (1990)

input: The class watched a fire-drill video while Owen was in the nurse's office. If a teacher asks the class what to do during a fire drill, why might Owen struggle to answer correctly?
target: Owen might struggle because he missed the video that taught everyone else the fire-drill steps -- he simply wasn't exposed to that information, unlike his classmates.

metadata.rubric: Must explain his struggle is due to missing the informational source (the video), not because he's careless.
metadata.literature_basis: Wimmer, Hogrefe & Perner (1988) Seeing-Leads-to-Knowing; Pratt & Bryant (1990)

input: Ines and Paul are handed sealed envelopes. Ines is allowed to open hers and read the letter inside. If asked what Ines's letter says, what should Paul say, and why?
target: Paul should say he doesn't know, because he never got to read the letter -- only Ines, who opened and read it, actually has that knowledge.

metadata.rubric: Must indicate Paul doesn't know AND explain it's because he didn't read the letter himself.
metadata.literature_basis: Wimmer, Hogrefe & Perner (1988) Seeing-Leads-to-Knowing; Pratt & Bryant (1990)

input: Sally puts her marble in a basket and leaves. While she's out, Anne moves the marble to a box. When Sally returns, where will she look first, and why?
target: Sally will look in the basket first, because that's where she left the marble and she didn't see Anne move it -- she's acting on her last known information, not the current reality.

metadata.rubric: Must say basket AND explain she doesn't know about the move (acts on outdated belief).
metadata.literature_basis: Wimmer & Perner (1983) Sally-Anne task; Perner, Leekam & Wimmer (1987) Smarties task

input: Maxi's mom moves chocolate from its usual place in a green cupboard to a blue cupboard while Maxi is outside playing. Where will Maxi look for the chocolate first, and why might he be wrong?
target: Maxi will look in the green cupboard first, since that's where he last saw it placed. He'll be wrong because he has no way of knowing his mom moved it while he was outside.

metadata.rubric: Must say green cupboard AND explain the false belief stems from not witnessing the move.
metadata.literature_basis: Wimmer & Perner (1983) Sally-Anne task; Perner, Leekam & Wimmer (1987) Smarties task

input: A delivery driver always leaves packages on the porch. Because it's raining today, he leaves the package in the mailbox. The homeowner, who missed the delivery, is expecting a package. Where will she check first, and why might she be surprised?
target: She'll check the porch first, since that's the usual spot, and she'll be surprised not to find it there because she has no idea the driver changed his routine today.

metadata.rubric: Must say porch AND explain the surprise stems from an unknown change in routine.
metadata.literature_basis: Wimmer & Perner (1983) Sally-Anne task; Perner, Leekam & Wimmer (1987) Smarties task

input: Every afternoon, the mail carrier leaves letters in the blue mailbox. Since the blue mailbox was full today, she used the red mailbox and forgot to leave a note. The homeowner wants to check for mail. Where will the homeowner check first, and why is this likely to fail?
target: He'll check the blue mailbox first out of habit, and it's likely to fail because he wasn't told about today's switch to the red mailbox -- his belief is based on past routine, not today's reality.

metadata.rubric: Must say blue mailbox AND explain the mismatch between habitual belief and unannounced change.
metadata.literature_basis: Wimmer & Perner (1983) Sally-Anne task; Perner, Leekam & Wimmer (1987) Smarties task

input: Noah leaves his plant on the balcony before school. A storm blows it indoors, and his mom moves it to the kitchen windowsill. Where will Noah look for it first when he gets home, and why?
target: Noah will look on the balcony first, since that's where he left it, and he has no way of knowing about the storm or his mom moving it while he was at school.

metadata.rubric: Must say balcony AND explain the false belief is due to being unaware of the storm/move.
metadata.literature_basis: Wimmer & Perner (1983) Sally-Anne task; Perner, Leekam & Wimmer (1987) Smarties task

input: John and Mary are at the park when the ice-cream van driver mentions to John that he'll be moving to the church later. John heads home. While he's gone, the driver changes his mind and parks by the school instead, and lets Mary know about the new plan, but Mary can't track John down to pass the message along.  Where does Mary think John will go looking for the van, and why?
target: Mary thinks John will go to the church, because she knows John never received the update about the school -- she can reason about what John still believes, even though she herself now knows better.

metadata.rubric: Must say church AND explicitly reason about Mary's model of John's (outdated) belief, not just what's true.
metadata.literature_basis: Perner & Wimmer (1985) Ice-Cream Van task

input: Liam mentions to his friend Noor that a surprise party is happening at the community center. After Noor left, the location changes to Liam’s backyard. According to Liam, where does Noor think the party is, and why?
target: According to Liam, Noor still thinks the party is at the community center, since she left before hearing about the change to his backyard. Liam has to track what Noor knows, not just what's currently true.

metadata.rubric: Must say community center AND frame it as Liam's belief about Noor's (unupdated) belief.
metadata.literature_basis: Perner & Wimmer (1985) Ice-Cream Van task

input: A magician tells his assistant the trick card is the Queen of Hearts, then switches it to the Ace of Spades. What card does the assistant think will be pulled, and why does this matter for the trick?
target: The assistant still thinks it's the Queen of Hearts, since she was never told about the switch. This matters because the trick depends on the assistant confidently expecting the wrong card, which helps sell the illusion.

metadata.rubric: Must say Queen of Hearts AND connect the assistant's false belief to why it serves the trick.
metadata.literature_basis: Perner & Wimmer (1985) Ice-Cream Van task

input: In the morning, Ms. Alvarez tells her class the field trip is to the zoo. Kofi leaves early with a belly ache, while Bea stays the whole day. By the afternoon, Ms. Alvarez annouces the field trip is now to the aquarium. If asked where Kofi thinks the trip is going, what should Bea say, and why?
target: Bea should say Kofi thinks it's the zoo, because that was the only announcement he heard -- Bea has to separate what she herself knows (aquarium) from what she knows Kofi believes (zoo).

metadata.rubric: Must say zoo AND make clear the answer is about Kofi's belief, not Bea's own knowledge.
metadata.literature_basis: Perner & Wimmer (1985) Ice-Cream Van task

input: Two business partners plan to meet a client at their downtown office. The client asks to move the meeting to a restaurant; partner A confirms this by email, but partner B's email stops working before he sees the message. Where does partner B think the meeting will be, according to partner A, and why?
target: According to partner A, partner B still thinks the meeting is at the downtown office, since B's email never came through with the update -- A must reason about B's unchanged belief, separate from the actual new plan.

metadata.rubric: Must say downtown office AND frame the answer as A's reasoning about B's belief.
metadata.literature_basis: Perner & Wimmer (1985) Ice-Cream Van task

input: Mia’s grandmother gets her a gift that Mia dislikes. When she receives it, Mia smiles and says she loves it. What is Mia likely feeling, and why does her expression not match it?
target: Mia is truly feeling disappointed, but she hides it and smiles instead because she wants to protect her grandma's feelings rather than show her real reaction.

metadata.rubric: Must name disappointment or frustration as the real feeling AND explain the mismatch is intentional, for grandma's sake.
metadata.literature_basis: Harris, Donnelly, Guz & Pitt-Watson (1986) Display Rules; Gross & Ballif (1991)

input: Sam strikes out and loses the game. Right after, he claps for the other team with a calm face. What is Sam likely feeling inside, and why is his outward behavior different?
target: Sam is likely feeling upset or disappointed inside, but he keeps a calm, sportsmanlike outward appearance to avoid seeming like a sore loser in front of others.

metadata.rubric: Must name upset/disappointed as the real feeling AND explain the display is a deliberate social choice.
metadata.literature_basis: Harris, Donnelly, Guz & Pitt-Watson (1986) Display Rules; Gross & Ballif (1991)

input: Aisha's dog just died. She confidently gives a class presentation with a steady voice right after she finds out. Does her steady voice mean she isn't sad, and what is she likely doing?
target: No, her steady voice doesn't mean she isn't sad. She's likely suppressing or hiding visible grief so she can get through the presentation, not because she doesn't feel it.

metadata.rubric: Must say she is still sad AND explain she's actively controlling her outward expression, not lacking the feeling.
metadata.literature_basis: Harris, Donnelly, Guz & Pitt-Watson (1986) Display Rules; Gross & Ballif (1991)

input: Omar loses a chess match to his little brother, shakes his hand, and says 'good game' with a smile. What might Omar actually be feeling behind that smile, and why might it be more than one feeling?
target: Omar might feel a mix of disappointment about losing and genuine pride in his brother, since both feelings can coexist even though only the smile is visible on the outside.

metadata.rubric: Must name at least two coexisting feelings (e.g., disappointment and pride) AND acknowledge mixed emotion is possible.
metadata.literature_basis: Harris, Donnelly, Guz & Pitt-Watson (1986) Display Rules; Gross & Ballif (1991)

input: The school nurse is giving flu shots to all the kids in a class. The first child winces and says it didn't hurt. Did the shot actually not hurt, and what is the child likely doing?
target: The shot likely did hurt, based on the wince -- the child is probably downplaying the pain to appear brave in front of friends, not accurately reporting how it felt.

metadata.rubric: Must say it likely did hurt AND explain the denial is about appearing brave, not the true experience.
metadata.literature_basis: Harris, Donnelly, Guz & Pitt-Watson (1986) Display Rules; Gross & Ballif (1991)

input: Priya trips in front of the whole cafeteria and everyone turns to look. Her face turns red. What is Priya feeling, and what specific cues tell you that?
target: Priya is feeling embarrassed. The cues are her face turning red, wanting to hide, and the fact that everyone is watching her after a public mistake.

metadata.rubric: Must name embarrassment AND cite at least one specific cue (blushing, wanting to hide, public attention).
metadata.literature_basis: Basic emotion recognition (Ekman); complex/social emotion recognition (Widen & Russell 2008)

input: After weeks of practice, Sam lands the skateboard trick in front of his friends. He grins and puffs out his chest. What is Sam feeling, and what cues show it?
target: Sam is feeling proud. His grin and puffed-out chest, along with finally succeeding after weeks of effort, are the cues that show this pride.

metadata.rubric: Must name pride AND cite at least one specific cue (grin, posture, or the effort-then-success context).
metadata.literature_basis: Basic emotion recognition (Ekman); complex/social emotion recognition (Widen & Russell 2008)

input: Marco accidentally broke his neighbor's window. Now every time he sees the neighbor, his stomach hurts and he avoids eye contact. What is Marco feeling, and why?
target: Marco is feeling guilty. His physical discomfort and avoidance of eye contact stem from knowing he did something wrong that he hasn't owned up to.

metadata.rubric: Must name guilt AND connect it to the unresolved wrongdoing/avoidance behavior.
metadata.literature_basis: Basic emotion recognition (Ekman); complex/social emotion recognition (Widen & Russell 2008)

input: Grandma’s voice sounds shaky and she pauses a lot as she shares news about her old friend over the phone. How does Grandma likely feel, and what tells you that, given you can't see her face?
target: Grandma likely feels sad. Even without seeing her face, her shaky, slow voice and the nature of the news (sad news about a friend) both signal sadness through tone alone.

metadata.rubric: Must name sadness AND cite vocal cues (shakiness, slow pace) as the basis, since facial expression isn't available.
metadata.literature_basis: Basic emotion recognition (Ekman); complex/social emotion recognition (Widen & Russell 2008)

input: Before his piano recital, Dylan's hands are clammy and shaky. He keeps checking the door and biting his lip. What is Dylan feeling, and what behaviors point to it?
target: Dylan is feeling nervous. The shaking hands, repeatedly checking the door, and lip-biting are all physical signs of anticipatory anxiety before a stressful event.

metadata.rubric: Must name nervousness/anxiety AND cite at least one specific behavioral cue.
metadata.literature_basis: Basic emotion recognition (Ekman); complex/social emotion recognition (Widen & Russell 2008)

input: The whole team is soaked because the sprinklers turned on during practice. Coach looks at the sky and flatly says, 'Oh great, perfect timing.' What does Coach actually mean, and how do you know?
target: Coach actually means the timing was terrible, not perfect. You can tell he's not sincere because of his flat, unimpressed tone paired with a clearly bad situation -- that mismatch is a signal of sarcasm.

metadata.rubric: Must state the intended meaning is negative/opposite of the literal wording AND cite the tone/context mismatch as evidence.
metadata.literature_basis: Winner & Leekam (1991); Filippova & Astington (2008) sarcasm comprehension

input: After the team loses 0-10, a teammate says, 'Yeah, that went great.' What is the teammate really communicating, and why say it this way?
target: The teammate is really saying the game went badly. Saying it sarcastically lets them vent frustration or make a wry joke about the loss rather than stating the obvious plainly.

metadata.rubric: Must state the real meaning (game went badly) AND offer a reason sarcasm is used instead of a direct statement.
metadata.literature_basis: Winner & Leekam (1991); Filippova & Astington (2008) sarcasm comprehension

input: The bus is 40 minutes late and it is pouring rain. A commuter mutters, 'Right on time, as always,' with a sigh. What is the commuter really saying about the bus, and what clues reveal this?
target: The commuter is really saying the bus is often late, the opposite of 'right on time.' The sigh, the obviously late bus, and the exaggerated phrase 'as always' all reveal the sarcasm.

metadata.rubric: Must state the real meaning (bus is often late) AND identify at least one sarcasm cue (sigh, contradiction with reality, exaggeration).
metadata.literature_basis: Winner & Leekam (1991); Filippova & Astington (2008) sarcasm comprehension

input: A student hands in ketchup-stained homework. The teacher glances at it and says, 'Very professional.' What is the teacher implying about the homework, and how can you tell?
target: The teacher is implying the homework looks messy and unprofessional, the opposite of what she said. You can tell she's not being literal because 'professional' clearly doesn't match a ketchup-stained paper.

metadata.rubric: Must state the implied meaning (messy/unprofessional) AND explain the literal words contradict the visible evidence.
metadata.literature_basis: Winner & Leekam (1991); Filippova & Astington (2008) sarcasm comprehension

input: After waiting two hours at the DMV, a man tells his friend, 'Well, that was fast.' What is he really saying, and why is does he say it like this?
target: He's really saying the wait took a very long time. It's sarcasm because 'fast' is the literal opposite of the two-hour wait he actually experienced.

metadata.rubric: Must state the real meaning (it took a long time) AND explain why the literal statement contradicts reality.
metadata.literature_basis: Winner & Leekam (1991); Filippova & Astington (2008) sarcasm comprehension

input: A fire station catches fire. Why is this situation funny, in your own words?
target: It's funny and ironic because fire stations exist specifically to fight and prevent fires, so it's an unexpected reversal for the fire station itself to burn. The outcome contradicts what you'd expect given its purpose.

metadata.rubric: Must articulate the contradiction between the fire station's purpose and the actual event.
metadata.literature_basis: Situational/verbal irony comprehension (Hancock, Dunham & Purdy 2000; Colston 2000)

input: A 'World's Best Driver' bumper sticker is on a car that just backed into a mailbox. Why might a bystander find this funny?
target: The bystander finds this funny and ironic because the sticker's confident claim directly contradicts the driver's clumsy mistake -- the reality (a bad driving moment) undercuts the boastful label.

metadata.rubric: Must explain the contradiction between the sticker's claim and the driver's actual poor performance.
metadata.literature_basis: Situational/verbal irony comprehension (Hancock, Dunham & Purdy 2000; Colston 2000)

input: A weather forecaster predicts a sunny picnic day, but it pours rain during the picnic. A friend says, 'Great forecasting.' Explain whether or not this is a genuine compliment, and why?
target: This is not a genuine compliment. It is ironic because the forecast turned out to be completely wrong, so praising the 'forecasting' actually points out the failure rather than genuinely complimenting accuracy.

metadata.rubric: Must state the compliment is not genuine AND explain how  the comment inverts the forecaster's actual (poor) performance rather than praising it sincerely.
metadata.literature_basis: Situational/verbal irony comprehension (Hancock, Dunham & Purdy 2000; Colston 2000)

input: A safety inspector's own building fails a fire-safety inspection. His colleague laughs. Explain why, in your own words.
target: His colleague laughs at the irony because the inspector's job is to ensure buildings are safe, so it's unexpected and contradictory for their own building to fail that very kind of inspection.

metadata.rubric: Must connect the inspector's professional role to the unexpected failure of their own building.
metadata.literature_basis: Situational/verbal irony comprehension (Hancock, Dunham & Purdy 2000; Colston 2000)

input: The display case of a store selling 'unbreakable' phone cases shatters when it falls. Why did the passersby cackle at this?
target: They laugh because it is ironic. The product is advertised as unbreakable, yet the very display meant to showcase that claim breaks, which directly contradicts the product's core promise.

metadata.rubric: Must connect the product's claim ('unbreakable') to the contradicting event (breaking).
metadata.literature_basis: Situational/verbal irony comprehension (Hancock, Dunham & Purdy 2000; Colston 2000)

input: Jamie gets an ugly haircut she doesn't like. She meets her friend Kayla, who says loudly, 'Whoa, who cut your hair, did you lose a bet?' and everyone laughs. Did Kayla mean to hurt Jamie, and what should Kayla have known, if anything?
target: Kayla didn't mean to hurt Jamie, as she didn't know Jamie already felt bad about the haircut, so her joke was an unintentional faux pas rather than deliberate meanness. Kayla couldn't have known this without being told, though she might reconsider joking about appearance in front of others in the future.

metadata.rubric: Must conclude the comment was unintentional (not deliberate cruelty) AND explain it stems from Kayla's lack of knowledge about Jamie's feelings.
metadata.literature_basis: Baron-Cohen, O'Riordan, Stone, Jones & Plaisted (1999) Faux Pas Recognition Test

input: At a dinner party, while looking at a large abstract painting on the wall, Mr. Lee says he dislikes modern art and thinks it 'looks like scribbles.’ His host had made the painting. Was this comment inappropriate, and why did it happen?
target: Yes, it was an inappropriate comment given who was present, but it happened because Mr. Lee didn't know his host was the artist -- it's an accidental faux pas caused by missing information, not intentional rudeness.

metadata.rubric: Must say the comment was inappropriate/hurtful in context AND attribute it to Mr. Lee's lack of knowledge, not malice.
metadata.literature_basis: Baron-Cohen, O'Riordan, Stone, Jones & Plaisted (1999) Faux Pas Recognition Test

input: During a group project, Priya says, 'Whoever wrote this part clearly didn't try very hard.’ Sam, sitting beside her, wrote it. What is Sam likely to feel, and did Priya intend to cause that?
target: Sam is likely to feel hurt or embarrassed. Priya didn't intend to cause that -- she made the comment without knowing Sam was the author, so the harm was accidental, not deliberate.

metadata.rubric: Must predict Sam's likely negative feeling AND explicitly state Priya didn't intend the harm.
metadata.literature_basis: Baron-Cohen, O'Riordan, Stone, Jones & Plaisted (1999) Faux Pas Recognition Test

input: At the office, Dan asks Rosa when her baby is due. Rosa isn't pregnant. Why is this an awkward moment, and what caused Dan's mistake?
target: It's awkward because Dan's assumption about Rosa's appearance is wrong and likely embarrassing or hurtful to her. His mistake came from an incorrect assumption, not from any real information about Rosa.

metadata.rubric: Must explain why it's awkward/hurtful for Rosa AND identify the root cause as Dan's false assumption.
metadata.literature_basis: Baron-Cohen, O'Riordan, Stone, Jones & Plaisted (1999) Faux Pas Recognition Test

input: At a wedding, Ines asks the groom's mother, 'Are you excited your son is finally settling down? We all worried he never would!' The mother begins to cry. Was this comment intentionally hurtful, and what should Ines have considered?
target: No, it wasn't intentionally hurtful. Ines simply didn't know about the mother's apparent sensitivity around this topic. In hindsight, she might have considered that comments about someone's personal history could be a sensitive area, even at a happy event.

metadata.rubric: Must conclude the comment was unintentional AND note the lack of awareness about the mother's sensitivity as the root cause.
metadata.literature_basis: Baron-Cohen, O'Riordan, Stone, Jones & Plaisted (1999) Faux Pas Recognition Test

input: Grandma knits Leo an ugly sweater. Leo says, 'I love it, thank you!' Why did Leo say this?
target: Leo said this to avoid hurting Grandma's feelings, not to deceive her for his own benefit. It's a kind, prosocial white lie meant to protect someone else's emotions.

metadata.rubric: Must state the motive is to protect Grandma's feelings AND classify it as non-harmful/prosocial.
metadata.literature_basis: Talwar & Lee (2002); Talwar, Murphy & Lee (2007) prosocial lie-telling

input: A coworker asks, 'How do I look before my big presentation?' Her outfit has a small stain, but there's no time to change. Her friend says, 'You look great, go get 'em!' Why might the friend choose not to mention the stain right now?
target: The friend likely avoids mentioning it because there's no time to fix it, and pointing it out right before a stressful presentation would only add unnecessary anxiety without any benefit.

metadata.rubric: Must explain the timing/no-benefit reasoning (nothing can be fixed, mentioning it would only cause stress).
metadata.literature_basis: Talwar & Lee (2002); Talwar, Murphy & Lee (2007) prosocial lie-telling

input: A child asks their parents if their elderly and sickly pet hamster will be okay. The parents say, 'The vet is taking good care of him.' Is this an honest answer, and why might the parents phrase it this way?
target: It's not the full truth, but it isn't meant to deceive maliciously -- the parents are softening a hard reality to protect the child from a difficult and premature worry, while still saying something true (the vet is caring for the hamster).

metadata.rubric: Must acknowledge it withholds the full truth AND explain the motive is protective/gentle, not deceptive for personal gain.
metadata.literature_basis: Talwar & Lee (2002); Talwar, Murphy & Lee (2007) prosocial lie-telling

input: Compare two situations: (1) a student tells a teacher 'I didn't copy that homework' when they did, to avoid punishment; (2) a student tells a friend 'I love your poem' when they think it's just okay, to be supportive. What's the key difference between these two lies?
target: The key difference is intent and beneficiary: the first lie protects the liar from consequences (self-serving), while the second lie protects someone else's feelings (prosocial) -- one is about avoiding blame, the other about kindness.

metadata.rubric: Must identify who benefits from each lie AND label one as self-serving/antisocial and the other as prosocial/kind.
metadata.literature_basis: Talwar & Lee (2002); Talwar, Murphy & Lee (2007) prosocial lie-telling

input: Dad burns the pancakes, but everyone says, 'These are great, Dad!' at breakfast. What is the main reason for this apparent lie, and what might happen if everyone told the truth instead?
target: The main reason to lie is to encourage Dad and not discourage him from cooking for the family. If everyone were blunt, Dad might feel embarrassed or stop wanting to cook, even though the lie has little real cost.

metadata.rubric: Must state the encouraging/protective motive AND speculate on a plausible negative outcome of blunt honesty.
metadata.literature_basis: Talwar & Lee (2002); Talwar, Murphy & Lee (2007) prosocial lie-telling

input: Comparing two kids who both broke a vase: Kid A was angry and threw a book at it. Kid B was running past and knocked it with her elbow. Should both kids be blamed equally, and why or why not?
target: No, they shouldn't be blamed equally. Kid A acted deliberately out of anger, while Kid B's action was unintentional. Most people judge intentional harm as more blameworthy than accidental harm, even though the outcome (a broken vase) is the same.

metadata.rubric: Must conclude they should NOT be blamed equally AND explain the distinction is based on intent, not just outcome.
metadata.literature_basis: Piaget (1932) intentionality in moral judgment; Nunner-Winkler & Sodian (1988)

input: A driver's foot slips off the brake and taps another car while parking. Did the driver intend to hit the other car, and how should we judge the driver?
target: No, the driver didn't intend to hit the car. It was an accident caused by a slip, not a deliberate action. This should make us judge the driver less harshly than if they had hit the car on purpose, even though there's still some responsibility for driving carefully.

metadata.rubric: Must say it was unintentional AND note this should lead to less severe judgment than a deliberate collision.
metadata.literature_basis: Piaget (1932) intentionality in moral judgment; Nunner-Winkler & Sodian (1988)

input: After Bobby’s mom tells him to clean his room, he throws a toy across the room in a fit of anger. The flying toy hits and breaks a lamp. Was breaking the lamp Bobby’s goal, and how does that affect his responsibility?
target: No, breaking the lamp wasn't Bobby’s goal. Throwing the toy in anger was intentional, but hitting the lamp was an accidental side effect. Bobby is still somewhat responsible for the risky action of throwing the toy, but less so for the specific outcome of breaking the lamp, since that wasn't the aim.

metadata.rubric: Must distinguish the intentional act (throwing) from the unintended consequence (breaking the lamp) AND note this nuance affects responsibility.
metadata.literature_basis: Piaget (1932) intentionality in moral judgment; Nunner-Winkler & Sodian (1988)

input: Jenny erased Kendra’s work on the shared whiteboard and called Kendra’s work stupid as she did it. Later on, Sally erases Nina’s work on the shared whiteboard because she thought it was her own turn to write there. Did Sally intend to erase Nina’s work? Should Sally be blamed the same as Jenny?
target: No, Sally didn't mean to erase Nina’s work, because it was a misunderstanding about whose turn it was, not a deliberate act. Sally shouldn't be blamed the same as Jenny who erased Kendra’s work on purpose to be mean. Sally’s intent was completely different, even though the result looks the same.

metadata.rubric: Must say it was unintentional/a misunderstanding AND conclude Sally shouldn't be judged the same as Jenny, who acted maliciously.
metadata.literature_basis: Piaget (1932) intentionality in moral judgment; Nunner-Winkler & Sodian (1988)

input: A cat scratches a child while trying to escape the child’s tight grasp. Did the cat intend to hurt the child? How should we interpret the cat’s behavior?
target: No, the cat didn't intend to hurt the child. It was reacting defensively to being held too tightly, not attacking out of aggression. We should understand this as a stress response rather than a deliberate or aggressive act.

metadata.rubric: Must say the scratch was unintentional/defensive AND frame it as a reaction to being held too tightly, not aggression.
